info.bio:
Mountain fue una banda excelente integrada por el guitarrista Leslie West, el bajista Felix Pappalardi, el baterista Cornky Laing y el teclista Steve Knight.
Lograron una magnífica mezcla de rock pesado y pasajes líricos, apoyados por letras inspiradas y hasta un diseño conceptual, obra de Gail Collins, la mujer de Pappalardi, la cual, por cierto, acabaría asesinándolo.

scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El hard rock marca el fin de los creativos sesenta: sigue basado en el blues, pero más rápido, ruidoso y fuerte, y entierra el sufrimiento negro bajo miles de decibelios. Precedido por Cream, Blue Cheer y Guess Who, lo definen Led Zeppelin, hijos del blues que lo tocan como música para el cuerpo y que imponen el LP como formato del rock. En Gran Bretaña, Free, Status Quo, Thin Lizzy, UFO, Uriah Heep, Slade, Faces, Deep Purple (el estereotipo del género), Black Sabbath (cimientos del black y el doom metal) y Queen, los bromistas del movimiento. En EE UU, Mountain, James Gang, Grand Funk Railroad, Montrose, Bachman-Turner Overdrive y Heart.

xref.title: The Rosary Murders (1987) – Uncredited Child Actor Appearance as Altar Boy
xref.body: While serving as an altar boy at the Church of the Holy Redeemer in Detroit, the young Jack Gillis (later Jack White) made an uncredited extra appearance in the 1987 film *The Rosary Murders*. He is visible in the film if you know where to look. This early exposure to acting contributed to his later interest in it as an adult, including a role in *Cold Mountain*. "Technically, this makes Jack White a child actor."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Bill Berry's Near-Fatal Tick Bite (May 1989)
xref.body: While R.E.M. was on tour in Germany in May 1989, supporting the "Green Album," drummer Bill Berry fell severely ill shortly after arriving in Munich. Initially suspected to be bronchitis or measles due to a rash, his condition worsened with hallucinations and fluctuating consciousness. Despite doctors' panic and a "huge buffet of antibiotics," the cause remained unknown until one doctor's blind prescription of tetracycline proved effective. Bill's doctor in Athens, Georgia, later diagnosed Rocky Mountain spotted fever, which Bill had contracted from a tick bite while gardening at home a week prior, and whose week-long incubation period had led to symptoms emerging during the tour. "Bill varies near fatal bug bites"

srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 7

xref.title: Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever – April 1989, Munich, Near-Fatal Illness Misidentified by European Doctors
xref.body: In April 1989, during a European tour, Bill Berry collapsed on stage in Munich with a fever of 103°F, chills, muscle aches, severe headache, nausea, red eyes, and a characteristic rash spreading from his wrists and ankles. German doctors, uncertain of the cause, prescribed tetracycline — the only antibiotic effective against Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever, a tick-borne illness virtually unknown in Europe that Berry had almost certainly contracted while gardening before the tour. Had the German doctors chosen penicillin (the standard first choice), Berry would have received no benefit and might have suffered organ failure, coma, and death. The correct diagnosis was only confirmed after his recovery. "It wasn't until later that it was determined that Bill had come down with something called Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Search for a Manager (1990)
xref.body: In the latter half of 1990, Nirvana was actively seeking a manager as they prepared to transition from an indie band to a major label, feeling clueless about the process. They met with several prospective managers, including Danny Goldberg of Gold Mountain Entertainment, who was very keen to sign them. Goldberg subsequently hired John Silva to meet with the band.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Rhyme and Reason Tour Cancellation (2000)
xref.body: In the summer of 2000, Rage Against the Machine planned a 30-date "Rhyme and Reason Tour" with the Beastie Boys, featuring activist messages and a promise to donate a dollar from every ticket to charity. However, the tour was entirely canceled after Beastie Boys member Mike D dislocated his shoulder in a mountain bike accident, rendering him unable to perform. "But then Mike D drove his mountain bike into a pothole and dislocated his shoulder. Turned out to be so bad that the whole tour had to be canceled."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Rhyme and Reason Tour Cancellation (2000)
xref.body: The Beastie Boys were scheduled to co-headline the 30-date "Rhyme and Reason Tour" with Rage Against the Machine in the summer of 2000, a tour intended to carry activist messages and donate to charity. The entire tour was canceled after member Mike D suffered a dislocated shoulder in a mountain bike accident. "In the summer of 2000, Rage announced that they were going to do a 30-date tour with the Beastie Boys called the Rhyme and Reason Tour... But then Mike D drove his mountain bike into a pothole and dislocated his shoulder."

xref.title: 'Unknown Pleasures' Cover Art
xref.body: The striking black cover design for "Unknown Pleasures" by Factory Records in-house art director Peter Saville featured minimal text and an image that appeared to be a mountain range but was actually a graphical representation (ridge line plot) of 100 consecutive pulses from CP1919, the first pulsar ever discovered, found in the Cambridge Encyclopedia of Astronomy. Saville reversed the original black-on-white diagram to white-on-black, creating an iconic image that launched countless t-shirts and a 2003 clothing line. "It was originally black on white, but Savile reversed it to be white on black. But what is this? It's a graphical representation, what's known as a ridge line plot, of 100 consecutive pulses from a pulsar known as CP1919."

xref.title: Battle of Bands Win Led to Bob Rock's First Ever Production Credit
xref.body: The band started as the K-Tels in 1978 in Vancouver but were threatened with legal action by the cheap record company K-tel International and renamed themselves Young Canadians. Frontman Art Bergman would remain a presence in Canadian alt-rock for decades, ultimately being made a Member of the Order of Canada in 2020. The band won a local Battle of the Bands contest that awarded them studio time at a new facility called Little Mountain Sound. The engineer assigned to these unknown contest winners was a young man named Bob Rock — it was the first time Rock ever produced anything. He went on to produce Metallica, Mötley Crüe, Bon Jovi, The Cult, the Tragically Hip, and many others. "The engineer assigned to them was some kid named Bob Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Death and Legacy
xref.body: Bruce Fairbairn passed away on May 17, 1999, at his home in Vancouver at the age of 49. Before his death, he established Little Mountain Sound in Vancouver, building it into one of North America's greatest recording studios. "On May 17, 1999, he was found dead at his home in Vancouver. It was just 49. But before he passed away, Bruce built his Vancouver recording studio, which is called Little Mountain Sound by the way, into one of the greatest recording studios in North America."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Career and Mentorship
xref.body: Rock was a top employee and assistant producer at Bruce Fairbairn's Little Mountain Sound studio, where he developed into Fairbairn's protégé. He initially performed longer than Fairbairn, working with Paul Hyde into the late 1980s. "But he also had an assistant producer job at Little Mountain Sound with Bruce and he became so good at his job that he became sort of Bruce's protégé."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Killed by His Wife
xref.body: Felix Pappalardi, the co-lead vocalist and bass player of Mountain, and a producer for bands like Cream and The Youngbloods, was murdered on April 17, 1983. He was shot to death by his wife, who used a gun that he had given her as a gift. He had previously suffered hearing damage while playing with Mountain. "But then on April 17, 1983, he was shot to death by his wife, who used a gun that he had given her as a gift."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Mentor to Bob Rock
xref.body: Bruce Fairbairn mentored Bob Rock, who started as an assistant producer at Fairbairn's Little Mountain Sound studio and later became his protégé. "Eventually, Bob started taking on his own clients and now his resume reads like some kind of who's who. ... And he got to where he is today thanks to the guidance and mentoring he received from another Canadian Superproducer, the late Bruce Fairburn."

xref.title: Proposed Cause of Death: Cardiac Episode
xref.body: In the opinion of the speaker, Taylor Hawkins died of a cardiac episode brought on by a previously diagnosed enlarged heart, which doctors were aware of but not concerned about, attributing it to years of intense drumming, mountain biking, and surfing, dubbing it a "runner's heart." "And in my opinion, he died of some kind of cardiac episode brought on by a previously diagnosed enlarged heart. A doctor knew all about it, but he wasn't worried, saying that all that heart muscle was the result of many years of intense drumming, plus mountain biking and surfing. They called this a runner's heart."

xref.title: Songwriting Credits
xref.body: John Denver is noted for writing well-known songs such as "Rocky Mountain High" and "Take Me Home Country Road," in addition to "Leaving on a Jet Plane." "Remember him, the American folk singer wrote songs like Rocky Mountain High and Take Me Home Country Road."

xref.title: Tour Interruption and Recovery
xref.body: After Bill Berry's emergency surgery, all R.E.M. shows were canceled for over two months. Berry recovered in the hospital for about a month, with the band members keeping him company and even smuggling in fresh donuts. The band returned to the stage with Berry on May 15, 1995, in Mountain View, California, and the official tour program for that leg featured an image of Bill's brain showing the aneurysms. "All shows were canceled until May 15th 1995 when Bill in the band returned to the stage in Mountain View California. The official program for that part of the tour featured an image of Bill's brain showing the aneurysms."
